content: Otitis media with effusion (OME) is a condition characterized by the accumulation of fluid in the middle ear cavity, which is particularly common in young children. This fluid can lead to hearing loss, and while most cases resolve spontaneously within a few months, persistent OME can result in behavioral issues and delays in expressive language development. Management strategies for OME include watchful waiting, medical treatments, surgical interventions, and other approaches such as autoinflation. Among the medical treatments, oral and topical steroids are sometimes used to reduce inflammation in the middle ear. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of using topical and oral steroids in children with OME. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials involving children aged 6 months to 12 years with either unilateral or bilateral OME. Comparisons were made between the use of steroids (oral or topical) and either placebo or no treatment. The primary outcomes assessed were hearing, OME-specific quality of life, and systemic corticosteroid side effects. Secondary outcomes included the persistence of OME, other adverse effects (such as local nasal effects), language and speech development, cognitive and psychosocial outcomes, listening skills, general health-related quality of life, parental stress, vestibular function, and episodes of acute otitis media. The review included 26 studies involving 2,770 children. Most studies on oral steroids used prednisolone for 7 to 14 days, while studies on topical (intranasal) steroids used various preparations, including beclomethasone, fluticasone, and mometasone, for durations ranging from two weeks to three months. All studies had some concerns regarding the risk of bias. Oral steroids compared to placebo: Oral steroids likely result in little to no difference in the proportion of children with normal hearing after 12 months. In one study involving 332 participants, 69.7% of children treated with steroids achieved normal hearing compared to 61.1% of those receiving placebo (risk ratio [RR] 1.14, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.97 to 1.33; moderate-certainty evidence). There is likely little to no difference in OME-specific quality of life, as measured by the OM8-30 score (mean difference [MD] 0.07, 95% CI -0.2 to 0.34; 1 study, 304 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Oral steroids may reduce the number of children with persistent OME at 6 to 12 months, but the size of the effect is uncertain. The absolute risk reduction ranged from 13.3% to 45%, with a number needed to treat (NNT) of 3 to 8 (low-certainty evidence). The evidence regarding the risk of systemic corticosteroid side effects was very uncertain, and no meta-analysis could be conducted for this outcome. Oral steroids compared to no treatment: Oral steroids may result in little to no difference in the persistence of OME after 3 to 9 months. In two studies involving 258 participants, 74.5% of children receiving steroids had persistent OME compared to 73% of those receiving no treatment (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.17; low-certainty evidence). The evidence on adverse effects was very uncertain. No evidence was identified regarding hearing outcomes or disease-related quality of life. Topical (intranasal) steroids compared to placebo: No data were available on the proportion of children who returned to normal hearing. However, one study involving 78 participants reported a mean change in hearing threshold after two months of -0.3 dB (95% CI -6.05 to 5.45; very low-certainty evidence). Nasal steroids likely make little to no difference in disease-specific quality of life after nine months (OM8-30 score, MD 0.05 higher, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.46; 1 study, 82 participants; low-certainty evidence). The evidence regarding the persistence of OME at up to one year was very uncertain. Two studies involving 206 participants reported conflicting results, with one study suggesting a benefit for nasal steroids and the other showing a benefit with placebo. The evidence on corticosteroid-related side effects was very uncertain, and no pooled effect estimate could be provided. Topical (intranasal) steroids compared to no treatment: No data were available on the proportion of children who returned to normal hearing. However, one study involving 168 participants reported a mean difference in final hearing threshold after four weeks of -1.95 dB (95% CI -3.85 to -0.05; low-certainty evidence). Nasal steroids may reduce the persistence of OME after eight weeks, but the evidence was very uncertain. In two studies involving 134 participants, 58.5% of children receiving steroids had persistent OME compared to 81.3% of those without treatment (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.91). No evidence was identified regarding disease-related quality of life or adverse effects. Conclusions: Oral steroids may have little effect on the treatment of OME, with minimal improvement in the number of children achieving normal hearing and no significant impact on quality of life. There may be a reduction in the proportion of children with persistent OME after 12 months, but this benefit is likely small and must be weighed against the potential for adverse effects associated with oral steroid use. The evidence for nasal steroids is of low or very low certainty, making it unclear whether they have any meaningful impact on hearing, quality of life, or the persistence of OME. Evidence on adverse effects is also very limited. Given that OME is likely to resolve spontaneously in most children, the potential benefits of treatment are small and should be carefully balanced against the risks of adverse effects. Future research should focus on identifying which children are most likely to benefit from treatment rather than offering interventions to all children indiscriminately.
